newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Juncker seeks reading of EMU pact that suits all.
newsitem.headline: Juncker seeks reading of EMU pact that suits all.

text.p: Luxembourg Finance Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, pointing to a possible way to assuage French fears about the EU's "stability pact", said on Sunday Europe would have to find an interpretation of the pact that suited everyone.

He was speaking ahead of a meeting of EU finance ministers on Sunday and Monday at which France's new Socialist-led government was expected to explain its position on Europe's planned economic and monetary union.
"We will listen to what (French Finance Minister Dominique) Strauss-Kahn has to tell us and we will see," Juncker said.
"Even if we do not manage to have a legal adoption of this (stability pact) text tomorrow, it is not a drama. The new minister has the right to express himself," Juncker said.
He told reporters he had "some indications" on the French position on the pact, meant to limit budget deficits after the launch of the single currency, but gave no details.
Strauss-Kahn made no comment as he arrived at the talks, except to say "we will see tomorrow". The stability pact was not due to be discussed until Monday.

But new French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who has pledged to fight against austerity in Europe, said during the campaign which swept the Socialists to power in a parliamentary election last Sunday, that he did not feel bound by the stability pact, agreed in Dublin last December.
Any attempt to renegotiate the pact could create a diplomatic crisis with Germany, which sees it as a guarantee of fiscal discipline after the launch of the euro in 1999.
Juncker said the pact was meant to ensure that the values of economic stability were enshrined in EMU.
"We have to see with the stability pact if we can reach an interpretation which suits everybody," he said.

Economists have suggested that France's new government might leave the body of the stability pact intact, but insist on adding some new wording which places the emphasis on fighting for growth and employment.
It could also look for further moves towards a European economic government which would define policies in euro zone meant to boost growth and lower unemployment.
Juncker said that the stability pact, which would impose fines on countries which allowed their budget deficits to overshoot a target of three percent of gross domestic product, was not anti-growth.
An agreement on the pact last year, under which fines will be imposed "as a rule" but not always, was meant to prevent these fines depressing growth further, he said.
France's previous centre-right government had insisted that the imposition of fines take account of economic recessions, watering down an original German insistence that the fines must be automatic.

Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn said he did not see any change to the terms of the pact to be changed during the Luxembourg talks. "As regards the terms of the stability pact, I don't expect they will be changed," he told reporters.
The pact had been due to be approved by EU heads of state and government at a summit meeting in Amsterdam next weekend.
Finish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto told reporters he thought the pact would be approved in Amsterdam.

But while financial markets have been focusing on the Luxembourg talks for a clear indication of France's views, French officials have suggested there may have to be talks with Germany before any position can be finalised.

Jospin is due to meet German Chancellor Helmut Kohl at a Franco-German summit in Poitiers, western France, on Friday, which will also be attended by French President Jacques Chirac and foreign and finance ministers of both countries.
